claims.text: A conventional W–Cu composite with direct W–Cu contact has relatively high interfacial thermal resistance.
A conformal Mo interlayer approximately 10–50 nm thick can be introduced at W–Cu interfaces during fabrication.
The Mo interlayer acts as a bridging phase at the W–Cu interface.
The Mo interlayer improves interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
The Mo interlayer reduces lattice mismatch at the W–Cu interface.
The Mo layer provides a graded W–Mo–Cu interface.
The Mo interlayer reduces phonon scattering at the W–Cu junction.
The Mo interlayer reduces electron scattering at the W–Cu junction.
Improved atomic coupling produced by the Mo layer lowers interfacial thermal resistance.
Lower interfacial thermal resistance increases the overall thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
A thin Mo interlayer can increase thermal conductivity without detrimentally affecting mechanical strength.
A thin Mo interlayer can increase thermal conductivity without detrimentally affecting irradiation stability.
A Mo-interlayer W–Cu composite will have a statistically significant increase in overall thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise identical uncoated W–Cu composite.
A Mo-interlayer W–Cu composite will retain mechanical durability comparable to an otherwise identical uncoated composite.
A Mo-interlayer W–Cu composite will retain resistance to irradiation-induced damage comparable to an otherwise identical uncoated composite.
The proposed effect applies under the high thermal gradients, mechanical stresses, and irradiation associated with heat-dissipation and fusion-reactor joint applications.
The beneficial effect requires the Mo layer to remain uniformly thin and continuous.
Nonuniformity or unsuitable thickness of the Mo coating may create defects that compromise mechanical integrity.
Nonuniformity or unsuitable thickness of the Mo coating may compromise irradiation resistance.
The magnitude of the conductivity enhancement may depend on processing conditions and Mo-layer thickness.
